title: Strict-local comparison reduced to a geometric strict-local fibre
statement: Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme], let $\bar x$ be a geometric point of $X$, and let $\bar s=f\bar x$ [def-weil-geometric-point]. Put $A=S_{(\bar s)}$ and $B=X_{(\bar x)}$ [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit], with their canonical map $h:B\to A$ [lem-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-functoriality]. Let $K$ be any separably closed field [def-pc-separably-closed], let $u:\operatorname{Spec}K\to A$ be a morphism, and write $t:\operatorname{Spec}K\to S$ for its composite with the structural map of $A$. Let $F$ be an abelian etale sheaf on $\operatorname{Spec}K$ [def-weil-pbc-abelian-etale-sheaves], and let $q\geq0$. Then the canonical pullback map [def-weil-pbc-cohomology-pullback] $$H^q(A\times_S\operatorname{Spec}K,F)\longrightarrow H^q(B\times_S\operatorname{Spec}K,F)$$ is an isomorphism if and only if, for EVERY morphism $v:\operatorname{Spec}K\to A$ whose composite with $A\to S$ is $t$, the canonical pullback map $$H^q(\operatorname{Spec}K,F)\longrightarrow H^q(B\times_{A,v}\operatorname{Spec}K,F)$$ is an isomorphism. Fibre products are those of [def-pc-fibre-product], and on each scheme the coefficients are the inverse image [def-weil-pbc-inverse-image] of $F$ under the projection to $\operatorname{Spec}K$; cohomology is [def-weil-pbc-etale-cohomology]. In particular, the first comparison implies the second comparison for the originally selected $u$. No smoothness, properness, finite-type, torsion, or algebraicity condition on $u$ or $v$ is assumed.

proof.text: Set $T=\operatorname{Spec}K$, $E=A\times_ST$, $Y=B\times_ST$, $p=h\times_ST:Y\to E$, and $a:E\to T$. Choose an affine open chart of $S$ containing $\bar s$; $t$ factors through it because it factors through the local scheme $A$ and any open containing its closed point contains all its points. In the strict-local limit one can restrict to pointed affine neighbourhoods mapping into this chart: pull back any neighbourhood along the chart and choose an affine open containing its distinguished point. By the defining ring colimit for $A$ and the universal properties of tensor products and colimits, $E=\operatorname{Spec}C$ with $C=\varinjlim_i C_i$, where $C_i$ are etale $K$-algebras obtained by base change of these affine etale neighbourhoods. Concretely, a compatible family of maps from their tensors to a $K$-algebra is exactly a compatible family of maps from the original coordinate rings agreeing on the chart ring. Etale base change and the finite-separable-product theorem, followed by triviality of finite separable extensions of $K$, give $C_i\cong K^{I_i}$ for finite sets $I_i$. The limit interpretation is justified by the small-colimit spectrum theorem. These decompositions are as $K$-algebras, NOT as $A$-algebras; no claim that different $v$ give the same $A$-fibre is made.

source.place: Tag 0EZV, first paragraph; Algebra Tag 00U3; Limits Tag 01YW

proof.text: For every prime $z$ of $C$, its pullback to each finite product $K^{I_i}$ selects a unique factor, by the finite-product spectrum statement. If $c\in C$ is represented by $(\lambda_j)_j\in K^{I_i}$ and the selected factor is $j_0$, the corresponding idempotent $e_{j_0}$ is outside $z$ and kills $c-\lambda_{j_0}$. Consequently every element of $C_z$ is a scalar in $K$: denominators outside $z$ have nonzero selected scalar and can be inverted in $K$. The structural map $K\to C_z$ is injective since it is a map from a field to a nonzero local ring. Thus $C_z\cong K$, compatibly with the structural maps. Every prime is therefore maximal, and the zero-dimensional spectrum theorem makes $|E|$ profinite. Points of $E$ are exactly $K$-morphisms $T\to E$, equivalently lifts $v:T\to A$ of $t$, since each residue field is canonically $K$. The given $u$ supplies one such point, so $E$ is nonempty. Finite stages can have unused factors; no surjectivity of their transition maps is assumed.

source.place: Tag 0EZV, finite-product presentation; Algebra Tags 00ED and 04MG

proof.text: For each $z\in E$, choose a geometric point $\bar z:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to E$ inducing an embedding $K=\kappa(z)\to\Omega$, with $\Omega$ algebraically closed. Clopen pointed neighbourhoods of $z$ are cofinal among the pointed etale neighbourhoods of $\bar z$. Indeed choose an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}D$ around the distinguished point of such a neighbourhood. Its fibre $D\otimes_C K$ is etale over $K$ by etale base change; the finite-separable-product theorem and separable closedness identify it with a finite product of copies of $K$. Thus its given map to $\Omega$ selects a factor and comes from a $K$-point: the pointed map $D\to\Omega$ factors through $D\to K=C_z$. By the affine-etale ring criterion, $D$ is a finitely presented $C$-algebra. Write the finitely many generator images in $C_z$ as fractions and invert the product of their denominators, all outside $z$. Each defining relation vanishes in $C_z$, so invert one further element outside $z$ annihilating it, for each of the finitely many relations. This produces a $C$-map $D\to C_s$, $s\notin z$, hence a section over $D(s)$ through the prescribed point. The clopen basis supplies $z\in W\subseteq D(s)$, and restriction gives a pointed map $W\to\operatorname{Spec}D$. By the clopen-idempotent theorem, each such $W$ is $D(e)=\operatorname{Spec}C_e$ for an idempotent $e$ of $C$, so it is an affine etale neighbourhood. Two such clopen refinements have common refinement their intersection. To equalize two pointed maps from a clopen into a neighbourhood, first shrink around $z$ into an affine open of that neighbourhood containing their common distinguished point. On its finitely many algebra generators the two maps have differences zero in $C_z$; invert finitely many annihilators outside $z$ and take a smaller clopen. The maps then agree, since they agree on every generator. This proves cofinality, including the equalization condition, for every choice of $\Omega$ and embedding $K\to\Omega$. Hence the stalk of any abelian sheaf at $\bar z$ is computed on the same clopen system, independently of $\Omega$. A germ has a representative on a clopen $W$; gluing it with the zero section on the disjoint open complement gives a global section with that germ. Therefore $\Gamma(E,G)=0$ implies that every geometric stalk of $G$ vanishes, and geometric-stalk conservativity gives $G=0$. The argument also applies to $T=\operatorname{Spec}K$; its clopen neighbourhood system has the single nonempty object $T$, so for every geometric point of $T$ the germ map $F(T)\to F_{\bar t}$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Tags 09AY and 03PN; clopen basis from Topology Tag 08ZZ; explicit localization argument; Algebra Tag 00EE, lemma-disjoint-decomposition

proof.text: Every point of the affine scheme $E$ is closed and every residue field is the separably closed field $K$, by step 2. Apply the affine closed-point acyclicity theorem to EVERY abelian sheaf on $E$: all positive right derived functors of $\Gamma(E,-)$ vanish. The category of abelian etale sheaves has enough injectives by [lem-weil-pbc-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]; global sections is additive and left exact since evaluation preserves kernels. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-derived-functor-long-exact] to a short exact sequence: its segment $\Gamma(E,G_1)\to\Gamma(E,G_2)\to\Gamma(E,G_3)\to H^1(E,G_1)=0$ therefore says $\Gamma(E,-)$ is exact. Combined with the zero-detection argument of step 3, it reflects isomorphisms: a sheaf morphism has invertible global sections precisely when its kernel and cokernel have zero global sections, precisely when both vanish. The same acyclicity theorem applies to $T$, so $H^q(T,F)=0$ for $q>0$.

source.place: Tag 09AY, lemma-affine-only-closed-points; derived.tex Tag 015B, lemma-higher-derived-functors (1),(2); injectives.tex Tag 01DU, theorem-sheaves-modules-injectives

proof.text: Put $G=a^{-1}F$. The map $p$ is affine: both $E$ and $Y$ are affine schemes, and $p$ is induced by their coordinate-ring homomorphism. Hence it is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. The canonical Leray comparison for $p$, with the explicit derived-unit description of cohomology pullback, identifies $H^q(Y,p^{-1}G)$ with $\Gamma(E,R^qp_*p^{-1}G)$, because exactness of $\Gamma(E,-)$ lets it commute with kernels, images and cokernels of a representing complex. For $q=0$ the first comparison in the statement is $\Gamma(E,\eta)$ for the unit $\eta:G\to p_*p^{-1}G$. It is invertible iff $\eta$ is an isomorphism by step 4. For $q>0$ its source vanishes and it is invertible iff $\Gamma(E,R^qp_*p^{-1}G)=0$, iff $R^qp_*p^{-1}G=0$. Composition of inverse images identifies $p^{-1}G$ with the coefficient sheaf pulled back from $T$ to $Y$. Thus we have reduced the first comparison to a sheaf isomorphism in degree zero or a sheaf vanishing in positive degree, without any torsion assumption.

source.place: Tag 03Q9, injective-complex paragraph; derived-unit Leray description

proof.text: Fix $z\in E$, equivalently a lift $v:T\to A$, and a geometric point $\bar z:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to E$ over it as in step 3. Cofinality of the clopen neighbourhoods from step 3 identifies the strict localization of $E$ at $\bar z$ with $\operatorname{Spec}C_z=T$: the clopen-idempotent theorem writes each affine clopen as $D(e)=\operatorname{Spec}C_e$. The ring colimit of these $C_e$ is the ordinary localization $C_z$: its natural map to $C_z$ is surjective since every fraction $c/s$ is defined on a clopen inside $D(s)$, and is injective since a section zero in $C_z$ is annihilated by some element outside $z$ and becomes zero on a smaller clopen inside its basic open. Thus the ring colimit over pointed etale neighbourhoods is $C_z$, since every denominator outside $z$ is inverted on a clopen neighbourhood contained in its basic open, and step 2 identifies that localization with $K$. The unrestricted strict-henselization stalk theorem applies to the affine, hence qcqs, morphism $p$ and the abelian sheaf $p^{-1}G$. It gives $(R^qp_*p^{-1}G)_{\bar z}\cong H^q(Y\times_E T,F)$. Fibre-product associativity, checked by their projections, identifies $Y\times_E T$ with $B\times_{A,v}T$. By the inverse-image stalk-and-germ theorem for $a:E\to T$, the source stalk $G_{\bar z}$ is $F_{a\bar z}$; step 3 on $T$ identifies this canonically with $F(T)=H^0(T,F)$. For $q=0$ the stalk of $\eta$ is the section-pullback unit $H^0(T,F)\to H^0(B\times_{A,v}T,F)$: a clopen representative of a germ restricts along the section in step 3, and its unit image restricts along the base-changed section, giving exactly the fibre pullback. For $q>0$, $H^q(T,F)=0$ by step 4, so the fibre comparison is invertible exactly when this higher-direct-image stalk vanishes. The clopen system is independent of the chosen $\Omega$ by step 3, so these identifications hold for every geometric point over $z$. This identifies the actual canonical maps, not just abstract groups.

source.place: Tag 03Q9, theorem-higher-direct-images; corrected geometric-fibre calculation for Tag 0EZV; Tag 03Q1, lemma-stalk-pullback (3) and germ compatibility; Algebra Tag 00EE, lemma-disjoint-decomposition

proof.text: For $q=0$, geometric-stalk conservativity says that the unit in step 5 is an isomorphism iff its stalk map at EVERY geometric point of $E$ is an isomorphism. For $q>0$ apply the same statement to $0\to R^qp_*p^{-1}G$, so vanishing is equivalent to vanishing at EVERY geometric stalk. By steps 2, 3 and 6 these conditions are precisely the comparisons for every lift $v:T\to A$ over $t$. This proves the corrected equivalence and, by taking $v=u$, the one-way implication needed by the existing smooth-local-acyclicity citer. The original assertion for only one selected lift is false; the nodal-curve counterexample and the invalid $A$-linear identification in the source are recorded in report.md.
